script.en:
CLERK: Good afternoon, Ashford Community Hall. How can I help?
CALLER: Hello. I'd like to book the hall for a party, please. It's for my daughter's eighteenth birthday.
CLERK: Lovely. We have two rooms, the main hall and the garden room. How many guests are you expecting?
CALLER: About forty. Well, my daughter says fifty now, so let's say fifty.
CLERK: Then it will have to be the main hall. The garden room only takes thirty-five people. Which date did you have in mind?
CALLER: Saturday the twelfth of July.
CLERK: Let me look. I'm afraid the main hall is already booked that day. Is the following Saturday any good? That's the nineteenth.
CALLER: Yes, the nineteenth is fine.
CLERK: Good. Can I take your name?
CALLER: Yes, it's Martin Fairclough.
CLERK: Could you spell the surname for me?
CALLER: Sure. F-A-I-R-C-L-O-U-G-H.
CLERK: Thank you. And your address, Mr Fairclough?
CALLER: Twenty-seven Mill Lane, Ashford.
CLERK: Lovely. Now, the main hall costs eighteen pounds an hour on a Saturday evening.
CALLER: We'd need it from seven until eleven.
CLERK: So that's four hours, which comes to seventy-two pounds. We also ask for a deposit of forty pounds, and you get that back after the party if nothing is damaged.
CALLER: That's fine. Is there a kitchen?
CLERK: Yes, there's a kitchen with two fridges and a cooker, but no dishwasher, I'm afraid. You can borrow our plates and glasses for free, but please bring your own tablecloths.
CALLER: OK. And where can people park?
CLERK: There's no parking at the hall itself, and Mill Lane is too narrow. But guests can use the car park behind the library. It's free after six.
CALLER: Perfect. Thanks very much.

RECEPTIONIST: Lakeside Leisure Centre, good morning.
CALLER: Hi. I'm calling about the swimming club. I'd like to join.
RECEPTIONIST: Great. I'll fill in the form for you now. What's your name?
CALLER: Amy Thwaite.
RECEPTIONIST: Is that T-W-A-I-T?
CALLER: No, there's an H after the T, and an E at the end. So it's T-H-W-A-I-T-E.
RECEPTIONIST: Got it, thanks. And how old are you, Amy?
CALLER: I'm sixteen. Seventeen next month.
RECEPTIONIST: OK, so for now that's sixteen. And your postcode?
CALLER: It's BR4 7TX.
RECEPTIONIST: BR4 7TX. Thanks. Now, membership. Adult membership is twenty-two pounds a month, but you're under eighteen, so you pay the junior rate. That's fourteen pounds a month.
CALLER: Fourteen. That's fine. Are there lessons as well?
RECEPTIONIST: Yes. Beginners have their lessons on Tuesday evenings, and improvers on Thursday evenings. Can you swim already?
CALLER: Yes, but not very well. I think I'm an improver.
RECEPTIONIST: Then Thursdays are for you. One thing: for your first session you need to bring a swimming cap. They're compulsory in the pool now.
CALLER: Do I need a photo for the membership card?
RECEPTIONIST: No, we take your photo here at the desk. And the lockers take a one-pound coin, but you get it back.
CALLER: Great. Thanks for your help.

OFFICER: Northway Coaches, lost property. How can I help you?
PASSENGER: Hi. I left a bag on one of your coaches last week, and I'm hoping someone found it.
OFFICER: Let's see. Can I have your name first?
PASSENGER: It's Rosa Delgado. That's D-E-L-G-A-D-O.
OFFICER: Thank you. And which day did you travel?
PASSENGER: It was the second of October. No, sorry, the third. The Friday.
OFFICER: The third of October. Where were you travelling from?
PASSENGER: From Leeds, up to Kendal.
OFFICER: Could you spell that for me?
PASSENGER: Sure, that's K-E-N-D-A-L.
OFFICER: And do you remember your seat number?
PASSENGER: Yes, it was fourteen. One four. I was by the window.
OFFICER: Good. Now, tell me about the bag.
PASSENGER: It's brown, a medium size. I first thought I'd left my sports bag, but no, it was my leather bag, the one with a long strap.
OFFICER: A brown leather bag. And what was inside it?
PASSENGER: A camera, and two library books. My phone was in my pocket, luckily.
OFFICER: OK. If it's handed in, it goes to our office at the bus station in Kendal. You can collect it there from Monday to Saturday, between nine and five. We're closed on Sundays.
PASSENGER: Thank you so much.

ASSISTANT: Riverbank Bike Hire. Good morning.
CUSTOMER: Good morning. I'd like to hire some bikes for Saturday, please.
ASSISTANT: No problem. How many do you need?
CUSTOMER: Three. Two adult bikes and one for my son. Oh, wait. My sister's coming too, so make that four.
ASSISTANT: Four bikes. And what time would you like to collect them?
CUSTOMER: Is nine o'clock all right?
ASSISTANT: We open at nine, but Saturdays are very busy. If you come at a quarter to nine, I'll have them ready for you.
CUSTOMER: A quarter to nine, then. Lovely.
ASSISTANT: Can I have a name for the booking?
CUSTOMER: Helen Ruddock. That's R-U-double D-O-C-K.
ASSISTANT: Thanks, Mrs Ruddock. How old is your son?
CUSTOMER: He's six. Does he need a child seat?
ASSISTANT: At six, no. He can ride his own small bike, and a small bike costs the same as a child seat, five pounds a day. Adult bikes are twelve pounds a day.
CUSTOMER: That's fine. Do I need to bring anything?
ASSISTANT: Yes, we need to see a driving licence. A passport isn't enough, I'm afraid, because it doesn't show your address.
CUSTOMER: OK. Is there a good route for a child?
ASSISTANT: The coast road is lovely, but it has a lot of traffic. Most people take the path by the canal, but at weekends it's very busy. With a six-year-old, I'd go along the old railway line. It's flat, and there are no cars at all.
CUSTOMER: Perfect. See you on Saturday.

ADMINISTRATOR: Hello, Westbrook Arts Centre.
PARENT: Hi. I'd like to sign my son up for one of your summer art courses.
ADMINISTRATOR: Of course. What's his name?
PARENT: Leo Varga. Varga is V-A-R-G-A.
ADMINISTRATOR: Thank you. And which course is he interested in?
PARENT: He really wanted portrait painting.
ADMINISTRATOR: Ah, I'm sorry, portrait painting is already full. We still have places on landscape painting, and on pottery.
PARENT: He's not keen on pottery. Let's go for landscape painting, then.
ADMINISTRATOR: Landscape painting. Does Leo have any allergies we should know about?
PARENT: Yes, peanuts. He's allergic to peanuts.
ADMINISTRATOR: I'll write that down. The fee for the week is ninety-five pounds. That includes all the materials. They used to cost fifteen pounds extra, but not any more.
PARENT: Ninety-five. Fine. Is lunch provided?
ADMINISTRATOR: No, there's no café, so he'll need to bring a packed lunch. We do give the children fruit and water in the afternoon.
PARENT: OK. Where are the classes?
ADMINISTRATOR: Not in our main building on the high street. This summer they're in the old school on Bell Street, because it has bigger rooms.
PARENT: The old school on Bell Street. Got it.
ADMINISTRATOR: And on the last day, parents are invited to an exhibition of the children's work, at four o'clock.
PARENT: Great. Thank you.

ADVISER: Greenfield College, course information. Can I help?
CALLER: Yes, hello. I'd like to know about your evening language classes.
ADVISER: Certainly. Which language are you interested in?
CALLER: I was thinking of Spanish, but I've changed my mind. I'd like to do Portuguese, for beginners.
ADVISER: Portuguese for beginners. The new course starts on the twenty-second of September.
CALLER: The twenty-second. And which evening is it?
ADVISER: Mondays and Wednesdays. Classes used to start at half past six, but this term it's seven o'clock, because of the building work in the car park.
CALLER: Seven. OK. And how much is it?
ADVISER: The full price for a term is two hundred pounds. Students pay a hundred and eighty. Are you a student?
CALLER: No, I work. I'm a nurse at the hospital.
ADVISER: Then it's the full price, I'm afraid. Can I ask what you do, for the form? Oh, you said. A nurse.
CALLER: Yes. Do I need to buy a book?
ADVISER: No, the college gives you the course book. But please bring a dictionary to every class.
CALLER: That's easy. Thanks very much.

RECEPTIONIST: Good morning, Greenway Tennis Club.
CALLER: Hello. I'd like to join the club, please. I've just moved to the area.
RECEPTIONIST: Lovely. I can fill in the form for you now. What's your name?
CALLER: Grace Malloy.
RECEPTIONIST: Could you spell your surname for me?
CALLER: Of course. It's M-A-double L-O-Y.
RECEPTIONIST: M-A-double L-O-Y. Thank you. And have you played tennis before?
CALLER: Yes, for about six years, but not for the last two.
RECEPTIONIST: That's fine. We have a group for returning players on Tuesday evenings.
CALLER: Tuesdays are good for me.
RECEPTIONIST: Great. Now, would you like full membership, or off-peak? Off-peak is weekdays before five o'clock.
CALLER: I work during the day, so full membership, please.
RECEPTIONIST: Full membership. That's thirty pounds a month. Your first session with a coach is free, and your card will be ready at the front desk on Saturday.
CALLER: Saturday's perfect. Do I need to bring anything?
RECEPTIONIST: Just your own racket for now. We have balls you can use.
CALLER: Lovely. Thanks very much.

LIBRARIAN: Good morning. Can I help you?
MAN: Yes, I'd like to join the library, please.
LIBRARIAN: Of course. I just need a few details for the card. What's your first name?
MAN: It's Jonah. J-O-N-A-H.
LIBRARIAN: Thank you. And your surname?
MAN: Okafor. That's O-K-A-F-O-R.
LIBRARIAN: Lovely. And your date of birth?
MAN: The fifteenth of March. Oh no, sorry, the fifth. The fifth of March. I always say it too fast.
LIBRARIAN: The fifth of March. And what's your postcode?
MAN: It's TN6 3LW.
LIBRARIAN: TN6 3LW. Thank you. Your card will be ready in five minutes, and you can borrow up to ten books at a time.
MAN: Ten. Great. And how long can I keep them?
LIBRARIAN: Three weeks. You can renew them online if you need more time, but not if someone else has asked for the same book.
MAN: That's fair. Is the library open on Sundays?
LIBRARIAN: Only in the afternoon, from one until five. On weekdays we're open from nine in the morning until seven in the evening.
MAN: Thanks very much.

OFFICE: Hello, Castleford Tourist Office.
CALLER: Hi. I'm ringing about the guided walk round the old town. Is it on this Sunday?
OFFICE: Yes, it is. It starts at the castle gate. Last year it started at the museum, but the museum's closed for repairs now, so we meet at the castle gate.
CALLER: The castle gate. And what time does it start?
OFFICE: At ten o'clock. Oh, wait, I'm sorry, that's the summer time. In October it starts at half past ten.
CALLER: Half past ten. How long does it take?
OFFICE: About two hours, and there are a lot of steps, so wear good shoes.
CALLER: And how much is it?
OFFICE: It's eight pounds for adults, and five pounds for students.
CALLER: I'm a student, so five. Do I need to book?
OFFICE: No, just come along. You pay the guide on the day, in cash. The guide can't take cards.
CALLER: What happens if it rains?
OFFICE: The walk still goes ahead in light rain, so bring a coat. If the weather is really bad, we put a notice on our website by eight o'clock in the morning.
CALLER: Thanks a lot.

GUIDE: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to Greenway City Farm. My name's Nadia, and I look after the volunteers here. I'm going to tell you a little about how the day works, and then show you where everything is on the plan.
GUIDE: First, the timetable. We start at half past eight, not nine as it says on our website, because the animals have their breakfast early. Lunch is at half past twelve, and you'll finish at four.
GUIDE: Now, jobs. Most of you will spend the morning cleaning out the animal houses. It isn't glamorous, I know. In the afternoon, it depends on the day. On Saturdays, volunteers help in the farm shop, because that's when we're busiest. On Sundays a lot of families visit, so Sunday volunteers lead the tours for children. We used to ask volunteers to repair the fences as well, but we now pay a builder to do that.
GUIDE: One more thing. Please don't give the animals anything you've brought from home. Even a sandwich can make a goat ill.
GUIDE: Right, let's look at the plan. You came in through the main gate, in the middle of the bottom row. Straight ahead of you is the duck pond. The building on your left as you come in, next to the gate, is the farm shop. On the other side of the gate, on your right, is the café. At the far end of the farm, in the top left corner, you'll find the goat house. The pig sheds are in the top right corner, and between them, in the middle of the top row, is the barn, where we keep the hay. Oh, and the volunteers' room, where you can leave your bags, is the small building to the left of the pond.

MANAGER: Hello, and thanks for coming to this morning's event to celebrate the reopening of Riverside Park. I'm Greg Holt, the park manager. The work took eighteen months, a lot longer than we planned, mainly because the old bridge turned out to be in a much worse state than anyone expected.
MANAGER: So, what's new? The most popular thing so far has been the new playground, and the kids tell me the zip wire is the reason. The slides are the old ones, just repainted. We've also planted over two hundred new trees. And the café has reopened, run by the same family, although it now opens at eight in the morning instead of ten.
MANAGER: A few rules. Dogs are welcome everywhere in the park, except in the playground and the flower garden. Cycling is allowed on the main path by the river, but not on the paths through the woods, because they're too narrow.
MANAGER: Now, the map on the board here. We're at the main entrance, in the middle of the bottom row, and the river runs along the top. Just to your right as you come in is the playground, so you really can't miss it. Straight ahead of us is the big lawn. If you walk past the lawn, right up to the river, you'll find the flower garden, in the middle of the top row. The café is also by the river, but on the left-hand side, beside the old bridge. Up in the top right corner is the boathouse, which is still closed. On the right of the lawn, half way up, is the car park, and the woods are on the opposite side, to the left of the lawn. And down here on your left, by the entrance, there's a picnic area.

LIBRARIAN: Good afternoon, and welcome to the new Fenwick Library. I'm Paul, one of the librarians, and I'll be giving you a short tour. The building opened in May, and it's three times the size of the old library on Station Road.
LIBRARIAN: Before we walk round, a few things that are different from the old library. You no longer need to show your card to use the computers; you just type in your card number. You can borrow up to fifteen books now, not ten. And we stay open until eight in the evening on weekdays, although on Saturdays we still close at five.
LIBRARIAN: We also run some regular events. On Monday mornings there's a story time for children under five. On Wednesday evenings there's a reading group for adults, and on Fridays, students from the college come in to help older people with their phones and computers. That's one of the most popular things we do.
LIBRARIAN: Now, the ground floor. Have a look at the plan in your leaflet. We're standing in the entrance hall, in the middle of the bottom row. The information desk is straight in front of you, in the middle of the floor. The children's library is through the door on your left, in the bottom left corner. Behind the information desk, against the back wall, in the middle, are the computers. The quiet study room is in the top right corner, and the newspapers and magazines are in the top left corner, by the big window. Finally, the café is in the bottom right corner, to the right of the entrance hall.

EDUCATION OFFICER: Hi, everyone, and welcome to Family Day at the Hartley Science Museum. I'm Kate, and I'm one of the museum's education officers. Today is a bit different from a normal day, so let me explain.
EDUCATION OFFICER: First of all, every activity today is free, including the planetarium shows, which usually cost three dollars. The shows are at eleven, one and three, and each one lasts about twenty minutes. They fill up fast, though, so please collect a ticket from the front desk before you go up.
EDUCATION OFFICER: On the first floor, there are three hands-on workshops. In the morning, children can build a small robot. That one is for ages eight and up. After lunch, the workshop is about making slime, which the younger ones love. And at four o'clock, our scientist, Dr Marsh, will explode a pumpkin. Don't worry, it's very safe.
EDUCATION OFFICER: Let me tell you where to find things on the first floor, since that's where most of today's activities are. Look at the plan on the back of your ticket. When you come up the main stairs, you're in the middle of the bottom row. The planetarium is the big round room in the middle of the top row. To the left of it, in the top left corner, is the space gallery. The robot workshop is in the room just to your left as you come up the stairs, and the slime workshop is in the room on your right. The picnic room, where you can eat your own lunch, is in the top right corner. And there are toilets on both sides, half way along.

PRESENTER: Good morning, and here's some information for anyone going to the Ashworth Castle Summer Fair this weekend.
PRESENTER: The fair opens at ten on both days. On Saturday it closes at six, and on Sunday at five, an hour earlier, because the castle has a wedding booked for that evening.
PRESENTER: Tickets cost twelve pounds for adults if you buy them online, or fifteen at the gate, and children under twelve go in free. Parking is in the field next to the castle and costs five pounds a car, but there's also a free bus from the railway station every twenty minutes, and the organisers are asking people to use it if they can.
PRESENTER: This year there are some new things to see. The most exciting is the falconry show, with eagles and owls, at eleven and two o'clock each day. There's also a medieval cooking tent, where you can taste bread made the old way. The jousting, sadly, has been cancelled, because one of the horses has been hurt.
PRESENTER: If you'd like to find your way around, here's the layout. You come in through the main gate, at the bottom of the site. Right in front of the castle, in the middle of the top row, is the big stage. The falconry show is to the left of the stage, and the cooking tent is to the right of the stage. Half way up, on the left, is the children's area, and opposite that, on the right, are the toilets. On your left as you come in through the gate there's an information tent, and the food stalls are just inside the gate, on your right.

MANAGER: Hello, and welcome to your first visit to Parkside Sports Centre. I'm Laura, the duty manager, and I'm going to explain how the centre works before you start.
MANAGER: Your membership card gets you into the building, so please don't lose it. A new card costs eight pounds. The centre is open from six in the morning until ten at night, Monday to Friday, and from eight until eight at weekends.
MANAGER: You can book classes on our app up to a week in advance. The most popular class is spinning, on Tuesday and Thursday evenings, so book early. Yoga is on Monday and Wednesday mornings, and there's a new class called circuit training on Saturday mornings, which is good for beginners. If you can't come to a class you've booked, please cancel at least two hours before, or you'll have to pay a two-pound fee.
MANAGER: Right, let me show you around on the plan. We're in reception, in the middle of the bottom row. The sports hall is half way up, on the left. The studio, where most of the classes happen, is in the top left corner. The swimming pool is in the middle of the top row, and the gym is in the top right corner. The changing rooms are half way up on the right, between the gym and reception. There's a small café just to the right of reception, and the first-aid room is on the other side, to the left of reception.

ORGANISER: Hello, everyone, and thanks for coming along to the Brook Street clean-up day. I'm Sam, and I'll be organising things today.
ORGANISER: First, let me explain the plan for the morning. We're going to start with the playground, because the children use it every day. After that, we'll move on to the river bank, which is where most of the rubbish ends up. Finally, if there's time, we'll do the car park behind the shops.
ORGANISER: Now, equipment. Last year we asked everyone to bring their own gloves, but this year the council has given us gloves, so you don't need your own. What you do need is a water bottle, because it's going to be hot. The council has also lent us litter pickers, the long sticks with a grabber at the end, so nobody has to bend down all morning.
ORGANISER: Each group has a leader. Maria's group will collect plastic bottles, Tom's group will pick up glass, and my group will do general rubbish. When you finish, bring your bags to the green van by the gate.

WARDEN: Hi there, and welcome to Oakfield Campsite. Before you go and put up your tents, let me show you where everything is. Have a look at the map I've given you. We're at the entrance, in the middle of the bottom row, and the lake is at the top.
WARDEN: The first building on your left as you drive in is the shop. It sells bread, milk and firewood, and it's open until nine. Opposite the shop, on your right, is the office, where I am most of the day.
WARDEN: If you keep going up the main road, you'll reach the shower block, which is half way up on the left. It used to be on the right, by the playground, but we built a new one last spring, so ignore the old sign. The playground is still on the right, half way up, opposite the showers.
WARDEN: Your tent pitches are right at the top, along the lake, on the left-hand side, and the barbecue area is at the top on the right, next to the water. Enjoy your stay!

TUTOR: So, Maya, Daniel, how's the presentation on city bees coming along?
MAYA: Quite well, I think. We've been looking at different sources. Daniel found a documentary from the nineteen nineties.
DANIEL: Yeah, it was fun to watch, but honestly, a lot of what it says is out of date now. The rules about keeping bees in the city have changed completely since then.
TUTOR: Fair enough. What else?
MAYA: We interviewed a woman who keeps hives on the roof of a hotel. That was the most useful thing we did, by far. She told us things we couldn't find anywhere else.
DANIEL: I agree. And then there's a website run by a honey company.
MAYA: Which I don't trust at all. They want to sell honey, so of course they say everything about city bees is wonderful.
TUTOR: Good, that's the right question to ask about any source. And the textbook chapter I gave you?
DANIEL: It's clear, but it's about bees in general, not bees in cities. So it's a bit too general for us.
TUTOR: Fine. Now, what's your focus going to be?
DANIEL: I wanted to argue that every school should keep a hive.
MAYA: But we talked about it, and that's quite risky with small children around. So now we're going to focus on what ordinary people can do at home, like planting the right flowers on their balconies.
TUTOR: That's much easier to defend. What about visuals?
DANIEL: We thought about making a model of a hive.
MAYA: It would take weeks. We're going to use photos from our interview instead. She said we could.
TUTOR: Good. And when will you practise it in front of me?
DANIEL: Is Thursday OK?
TUTOR: I'm away on Thursday. What about Friday morning?
MAYA: Friday morning's fine.

TUTOR: Right, Leila and Tom, let's look at your survey plan. You want to find out how students get to the college.
LEILA: Yes. First, we'll do an online questionnaire for all the first-year students.
TUTOR: That's a good idea. It's quick, and you'll get a lot of answers. What else?
TOM: We wanted to interview about forty students as well.
TUTOR: Forty interviews? Each one will take you twenty minutes, plus the time to write it up. That takes too long for a four-week project. Ten would be plenty.
TOM: OK, ten, then.
LEILA: We also thought about counting the bikes at the gate every morning for a week.
TUTOR: Hmm. The college already has those numbers. The security office counts them every day. So that's unnecessary; just ask them.
LEILA: Oh, great. And Tom wanted to buy a small camera to film the traffic outside.
TUTOR: I'd say no to that. A good camera costs too much, and you'd need permission to film people anyway.
TOM: Fair enough.
TUTOR: Now, who are you going to ask? Just first-years?
LEILA: We said first-years, but actually, I think we should include the second-years too, because a lot of them live further away.
TOM: Agreed. First and second-years.
TUTOR: Good. And how are you going to present the results?
TOM: I wanted a pie chart.
LEILA: But we've got six different kinds of transport, and a pie chart with six parts is hard to read. I'd rather do a bar chart.
TOM: Yeah, you're right. A bar chart.
TUTOR: And when are you sending out the questionnaire?
LEILA: By the end of next week, so on Friday.
TUTOR: Make it Wednesday. Students don't read their emails on Fridays.
LEILA: Wednesday, then.

TUTOR: Ana, Ben, I've read the draft of your report on food waste in the canteen. It's a good start. Shall we go through it section by section?
ANA: Yes, please.
TUTOR: The introduction is fine, but it's nearly two pages. Nobody will read two pages before they get to the point. Cut it down to half a page.
BEN: OK, half a page.
TUTOR: Your method section is very clear. I wouldn't change anything there.
ANA: That's a relief. I wrote that bit.
TUTOR: The results are where I have a problem. You say a lot of food is thrown away, but you only weighed the waste on two days. You need more than that. A week at least.
BEN: We could weigh it for another week before the deadline.
TUTOR: Good. And the recommendations. At the moment they're at the very end, after the discussion. Readers in a hurry want them early, so put them right after the introduction, as a short list.
ANA: Right. Now, about the recommendations themselves. We had three ideas: smaller plates for all meals, a cheaper half portion, and a sign about food waste.
BEN: I thought the sign was the best idea, because it costs almost nothing.
ANA: But people don't read signs. I think the half portion would make the biggest difference.
TUTOR: Actually, I agree with Ana. Most of the waste you found was food left on the plate, so smaller portions deal with the real problem.
BEN: OK, I'm convinced. We'll put the half portion first.
TUTOR: And who will you send the report to when it's finished?
ANA: The canteen manager.
TUTOR: Yes, and send a copy to the student union as well. They can help to make it happen.

PRIYA: So, Owen, we need to decide how to split the work on the mill project.
OWEN: Right. I think the first thing is the old photographs at the town museum. I'm happy to go and look at those. I've been there before.
PRIYA: Great, you do the photos. What about the newspaper archive? The library has the old newspapers on computer now.
OWEN: Could you do that? I'm hopeless with those old fonts.
PRIYA: Sure, I'll do the newspapers. And the interview with Mrs Holden, the woman whose grandmother worked at the mill. I think we should both go to that. It's the most important part.
OWEN: Definitely. Two people can take better notes. What about the company's records, the ones in the city archive?
PRIYA: I phoned them. They're closed for two months, so neither of us can see them before the deadline. We'll have to leave them out.
OWEN: Shame. OK, what's our main question going to be? I liked "Why did the mill close?"
PRIYA: The teacher said lots of groups are doing why places closed. I'd rather do what working there was like for children, because Mrs Holden's grandmother started there at twelve.
OWEN: That's better, actually. More personal. Let's do that.
PRIYA: And how are we going to present it? A poster or a talk?
OWEN: The teacher said we could choose. I'd say a short talk, with the photos on a screen. A poster can't show many photos.
PRIYA: OK, a talk. And let's meet again on Tuesday to check how we're doing.
OWEN: I've got football on Tuesday. Wednesday?
PRIYA: Wednesday, then.

TUTOR: So, Sara, Jack, how did the field trip to Marsh End go?
SARA: Really well. The bird watching first thing in the morning was the best part. We saw herons, and I'd never seen one before. I really enjoyed it.
JACK: Me too. The water testing was harder than I expected, though. The kit had so many steps, and we got the first two samples wrong.
TUTOR: It's tricky the first time. And the talk from the warden?
JACK: Honestly, it was quite dull. He read from his notes for an hour.
SARA: I thought it was all right, but yes, it went on a bit.
TUTOR: What about the walk round the reed beds?
SARA: That was great, but it was over far too quickly. We only had twenty minutes, and there was so much to see.
TUTOR: OK. Now, your write-up. What will you focus on?

LECTURER: Good morning. Today I want to look at what happens to paper after you put it in the recycling bin, because it's a more complicated journey than most people think.
LECTURER: The first stage is collection and sorting. Paper arrives at the recycling plant mixed up with all sorts of things, and it's sorted into grades: newspapers in one group, office paper in another, cardboard in a third. This matters, because each grade makes a different product.
LECTURER: Next, the paper goes into a huge machine called a pulper. Here it's mixed with water and some chemicals, and stirred until it breaks down into tiny fibres. The result is a grey, wet mixture that we call pulp.
LECTURER: The pulp is then pushed through screens, which work a bit like sieves. They catch anything that isn't paper: staples, bits of plastic, and glue from envelopes.
LECTURER: Then comes de-inking. One common method uses air. Air is blown through the pulp, the ink sticks to the bubbles, and the bubbles rise to the surface, where the dirty foam is simply removed. If the paper is going to be white, it may also be bleached at this point. For brown paper and cardboard, this step is left out.
LECTURER: Now the clean pulp is ready to become paper again. It's sprayed onto a moving belt of fine mesh, and the water drains through. Then the wet sheet passes between heavy rollers, which squeeze out more water, and finally over heated rollers, which dry it. The finished paper is wound onto enormous reels.
LECTURER: One last point. Paper can't be recycled for ever. Each time it goes through the process, the fibres get shorter, and after a number of cycles they're too short to hold together. So some new fibre from trees always has to be added.

LECTURER: Today's topic is how people kept things cold before the refrigerator. It's easy to forget that the electric fridge only became common in homes in the twentieth century. Before that, the main answer was ice, and the problem was how to keep it.
LECTURER: The ice itself came from nature. In winter, workers cut blocks of ice from frozen lakes and ponds, using long saws. The blocks were then carried by horse and cart to an ice house.
LECTURER: An ice house was a special building, and the design was clever. It was usually built partly underground, because the ground stays cool, and often in the shade of trees. The walls were very thick, sometimes with two layers and a gap of air in between. Inside, the blocks were packed tightly together, and straw was placed between them and around them. Straw doesn't let heat pass through easily, so it slowed the melting. Some ice houses used sawdust instead, which worked just as well.
LECTURER: There was one more important feature: a drain at the bottom. Some ice always melted, and if that water had stayed inside, it would have melted the rest much faster.
LECTURER: With all this, a well-built ice house could keep ice until the end of the summer. Large country houses used it for cooling drinks, for making ice cream, and for keeping fish and meat fresh.
LECTURER: In the nineteenth century, ice even became an international business. Ships carried ice from North America to much hotter countries, packed in sawdust. The voyage could take four months, and a surprising amount of the ice was still frozen when it arrived.

LECTURER: This morning we're looking at plants that live in deserts, and the different ways they deal with the main problem of desert life, which is, of course, a shortage of water.
LECTURER: Let's start with the cactus, because it shows several tricks at once. First, its skin. A cactus has a thick, waxy skin, and the wax works like a raincoat in reverse: it keeps the water in. Second, the spines. Spines are in fact a kind of leaf. Ordinary flat leaves lose a lot of water, so the cactus has replaced them with spines, which lose very little. They also give a little shade, and of course they stop animals from eating the plant. Third, the stem. In a cactus it's the stem, not the leaves, that makes food from sunlight, and the stem can swell up to store water after it rains.
LECTURER: Now, roots. Many cacti have roots that are shallow, but spread out very wide, just under the surface, so they can take in rain quickly before it dries up. Other desert plants do the opposite. Some trees send their roots down very deep, to reach water far underground.
LECTURER: Timing is another trick. Plants take in gas through tiny holes in their surface, and water escapes through the same holes. Many desert plants open these holes only at night, when it's cooler, so they lose much less water.
LECTURER: Finally, some desert plants avoid the dry season altogether. Their seeds can wait in the soil for years. When rain finally comes, they grow, flower and make new seeds in just a few weeks, and then the plants die.

LECTURER: Today I'd like to talk about glass, a material we see everywhere but rarely think about.
LECTURER: Glass is made mainly from three ingredients. The most important is sand. Sand on its own melts only at a very high temperature, so the second ingredient, soda ash, is added to make it melt more easily. The third, limestone, makes the finished glass stronger and stops it from slowly dissolving in water. Today, a large part of the mixture is usually recycled glass, broken into small pieces. Because it melts more easily than sand, it saves energy, and that's the main reason glass makers want it.
LECTURER: The mixture is heated in a furnace to well over a thousand degrees, until it becomes a thick, glowing liquid.
LECTURER: For windows, most flat glass today is made by the float method. The hot liquid glass is poured onto a long bath of melted tin. The glass is lighter than the tin, so it floats on top and spreads out, and because the surface of the tin is perfectly flat, the glass becomes perfectly flat too. Before this method, flat glass had to be ground and polished by hand, which took a long time.
LECTURER: Next, the long ribbon of glass moves slowly through a long oven, where it's cooled very gradually. This step is called annealing. If glass cools too fast, the outside becomes hard while the inside is still hot, and the glass can crack later for no obvious reason.
LECTURER: Finally, the cooled glass is checked for faults by cameras, and then it's cut into sheets.

LECTURER: Today we're following coffee from the farm to your cup.
LECTURER: Coffee grows on bushes, and the part we use is the seed inside a small red fruit, which farmers call a cherry. Most coffee is still picked by hand, because the cherries on one branch don't all ripen at the same time.
LECTURER: After picking, the beans have to be taken out of the fruit, and there are two main ways of doing this. In the dry method, the whole cherries are spread out in the sun for a few weeks, and turned regularly so that they dry evenly. Then the dried fruit is removed by machine. This method needs very little water, so it's common in places where water is scarce.
LECTURER: In the washed method, the fruit is removed first, and the beans are left in tanks of water for a day or two, before they're dried. This uses a lot more water, but many buyers say it gives a cleaner taste.
LECTURER: Either way, the result is green coffee: hard, pale beans that keep well. This is the form in which coffee is shipped around the world.
LECTURER: The next stage, roasting, usually happens in the country where the coffee will be drunk. The beans are heated, they turn from green to brown, and they develop the smell and the flavour we know. A light roast keeps more of the bean's own character; a dark roast tastes more bitter and smoky.
LECTURER: Lastly, grinding. Once coffee is ground, it loses its flavour quickly, which is why many people grind their beans just before they make their coffee.

LECTURER: In today's lecture, I'm going to walk you through how a town might plan a safe network of cycle routes. To keep things simple, let's imagine a town of about fifty thousand people. I'll call it Eastbrook.
LECTURER: The planners' first step should always be to find out how people travel now. In Eastbrook, they'd count bikes and cars at busy junctions, and they'd ask people where they go every day. This is called a travel survey.
LECTURER: The second step is to choose priorities. Most towns start with routes to schools, because children are the people least able to protect themselves on busy roads, and because the trips are short.
LECTURER: Step three is design. On main roads, the best kind of cycle lane is a protected lane, which means it's separated from the cars by a kerb or a low wall, not just a painted line. Painted lines are cheap, but many people still don't feel safe using them. On smaller streets, separate lanes aren't usually needed; lowering the speed limit can be enough.
LECTURER: The fourth step is parking. People won't cycle to the station if there's nowhere safe to leave a bike, so secure bike parking at stations is essential.
LECTURER: And finally, step five: measure the results. In our imaginary Eastbrook, let's say the council counted three hundred cyclists a day on the main bridge before the changes. If the count rose to nine hundred two years later, they'd know the network was working, and they could use those numbers to ask for money for the next stage.

LECTURER: In this part of the lecture I want to explain how bees turn flowers into honey, in four steps. I'll start with a confession: I learned most of this from my neighbour, who keeps two hives at the end of her garden.
LECTURER: First, a worker bee visits flowers and drinks their nectar, a sweet liquid. She doesn't swallow it in the usual way. She keeps it in a special part of her body called the honey stomach, and carries it back to the hive.
LECTURER: Second, at the hive, she passes the nectar to younger bees who work inside. They pass it from bee to bee, and then put it into the six-sided cells of the comb.
LECTURER: Third, the nectar is still far too watery to be honey. So the bees fan their wings over the cells, which moves warm air across them, and slowly the extra water dries away. The nectar becomes thick and sticky. On a warm night, a busy hive can sound like a small motor.
LECTURER: Finally, when the honey is ready, the bees close each cell with a thin lid of wax. Sealed like this, honey keeps for a very long time, which is exactly what the colony needs to get through the winter.

LECTURER: Let's look now at how cocoa beans become chocolate, because it's a longer process than people expect.
LECTURER: The beans grow inside large pods on the cocoa tree. The first time I tasted a fresh bean, straight from the pod, I was amazed: it tasted nothing like chocolate, more like a sour lemon. After the pods are cut open, the beans and the white pulp around them are piled up and covered with banana leaves, and left to ferment for several days. This is where the first chocolate flavours start to form.
LECTURER: Next, the beans are dried in the sun, and then shipped to a factory. There they are roasted, which brings out the full flavour and the smell of chocolate.
LECTURER: After roasting, the thin shells are cracked and blown away, leaving small pieces of bean called nibs. Many people think the shells are what we eat, but it's the nibs that matter.
LECTURER: The nibs are then ground into a thick brown paste. Sugar is added, and milk powder too for milk chocolate. The mixture is stirred for hours to make it smooth, then cooled carefully and poured into moulds.

HOST: Welcome back to Campus Radio. My guest today is Claire Benton, who volunteers at the Fernhill Wildlife Rescue Centre. Claire, how did you get involved?
CLAIRE: Well, it was a bit of an accident, really. Two years ago I found a hedgehog in my garden that couldn't walk properly, and I took it to Fernhill. While I was there, I saw a notice asking for volunteers, and I signed up that afternoon.
HOST: And what do you actually do there?
CLAIRE: At first it was mostly cleaning, washing out cages and so on. These days I'm trusted with feeding the baby birds, which has to be done every half an hour in the spring, so it's a long day.
HOST: Every half an hour? That sounds exhausting.
CLAIRE: It is, but you get used to it. The hardest part isn't the work, honestly. It's letting the animals go. You get attached to them, and then one day they're ready, and you have to open the box and watch them leave.
HOST: What kind of animals do you get most?
CLAIRE: People expect foxes and badgers, but by far the most common patients are garden birds, especially young ones that have fallen out of the nest. Often they don't need rescuing at all. Their parents are nearby, still feeding them.
HOST: So what should listeners do if they find a baby bird?
CLAIRE: Watch it from a distance for an hour or so before doing anything. If the parents come back, leave it alone. Only call us if it's injured, or if you're sure no adult has come.
HOST: And how is the centre funded?
CLAIRE: Almost entirely by donations from people like your listeners. We get a small grant from the council, but it covers less than a tenth of our costs. Our biggest fundraiser is a sponsored walk every September.
HOST: Claire, thanks for coming in.

MEGAN: Hi, everyone. I'm Megan, and I spent last spring term as an exchange student at Harlow College, in a small town in the north of England. I was asked to tell you what surprised me most, so here goes.
MEGAN: First, the weather. Everyone had warned me it would rain all the time. Actually, it rained less than it does at home in Seattle. What nobody mentioned was the wind. Some days I could hardly open the front door.
MEGAN: Second, the food. I expected to miss American food, but the thing I really missed was a big breakfast on weekdays. My host family just had toast and tea, and by eleven o'clock I was starving. In the end I started keeping cereal bars in my bag.
MEGAN: Classes were different, too. At home, we have a lot of small tests during the term. At Harlow, almost everything depended on one long essay at the end, which was scary at first. But I found I learned more, because I had time to read properly.
MEGAN: The best part was the people. My host mother, Jean, had never been to the States, and she asked me hundreds of questions. We'd talk for hours in the kitchen. I still send her an email every week.
MEGAN: If you're thinking of doing an exchange, my main advice is this: don't fill every weekend with trips. I went to London four times, and it was fun, but the weekends I stayed in town are the ones I remember. That's when I really got to know people.

RANGER: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to Glenmore National Park. I'm Rob, one of the rangers. Before you set off on today's walk, there are a few things you need to know.
RANGER: The park covers mountains, forests and two large lakes, and it can be a dangerous place if you don't respect it. The weather on the high ground changes very quickly. It might be sunny down here at the visitor centre and freezing at the top, so even in summer, take a warm layer and a waterproof jacket.
RANGER: Phones don't work in most of the valleys. So before you leave, tell someone where you're going and when you expect to be back. For school groups, that means your teacher, who will leave your route with us at the desk.
RANGER: Now, wildlife. You may see red deer on the hills, especially early in the morning. Please don't try to get close to them for a photo; keep at least fifty metres away. And please don't feed the ducks on the lake. Bread isn't good for them, and it attracts rats.
RANGER: Fires are not allowed anywhere in the park, and that includes camping stoves on the hills, because the ground is very dry at this time of year. If you want a hot drink, bring a flask.
RANGER: Finally, rubbish. There are no bins on the trails. That's deliberate: bins attract animals, and they need emptying, which means more vehicles. So whatever you bring in, you take home with you.
RANGER: Right, let's get going.

NATE: Polly, did you get everything in the sleep lecture? I lost track in the middle.
POLLY: Most of it. Which part?
NATE: The bit about teenagers. She said our body clocks shift, right?
POLLY: Yes. During the teenage years, the body clock moves later, so teenagers naturally feel sleepy later at night, and want to wake up later. It's not just laziness, which I was glad to hear.
NATE: Ha. And she said something about screens.
POLLY: She said the light from screens in the evening can make it harder to fall asleep. But she was careful about it. She said the bigger problem is usually what we're doing on the screen, like messaging, which keeps the brain busy.
NATE: Right. Then there was the experiment she wants us to do.
POLLY: The sleep diary. For two weeks, we write down when we go to bed, when we wake up, and how alert we feel in the morning, on a scale of one to five.
NATE: Two weeks? I thought she said one.
POLLY: She said one at first, then corrected herself. It's two.
NATE: OK. And do we hand in the diary?
POLLY: No, just a one-page summary of what we found. She said she doesn't want to read our diaries, just our conclusions.
NATE: Fair enough. When's that due?
POLLY: Monday the eighteenth. And she said the next lecture is on dreams, so there's a chapter to read for that. Chapter seven.
NATE: Thanks, Polly. You're a lifesaver.

DAN: Welcome to Second Chances, the podcast about learning new things later in life. I'm Dan.
RUTH: And I'm Ruth. Today we're talking about learning a musical instrument as an adult, because I've just started the cello, at forty-two.
DAN: Brave! Why the cello?
RUTH: I wanted the violin at first, actually. But my teacher pointed out that the cello is easier on your neck and shoulders, because you sit down to play it. And I love the sound. It's closer to a human voice.
DAN: How are you finding it?
RUTH: Slow. Adults expect to be good quickly, because we're good at other things. Children don't have that problem. They're happy to sound terrible for a year.
DAN: So what's the secret?
RUTH: My teacher's rule is short and often. Fifteen minutes every day is better than two hours on a Sunday. I put the cello in the living room, out of its case, so I see it every time I walk past. That alone made a big difference.
DAN: I'd have thought a room of its own would be better.
RUTH: That's what I did at first, but if it's hidden away, you forget about it.
DAN: And lessons? Online or in person?
RUTH: I tried online, but the teacher couldn't see my hands properly, and with the cello, the position of the hands is everything. So now I go to her house every Wednesday.
DAN: Any goals?
RUTH: I'd like to join an amateur orchestra. There's one in town that takes beginners after their first year, so that's my aim for next autumn.
DAN: Brilliant. Good luck, Ruth.

TUTOR: So, Kai and Imogen, where are you with the packaging project?

IMOGEN: Three options. Paper boxes, boxes made from sugar cane fibre, and a deposit scheme with metal tins that customers bring back.
TUTOR: And what do you think of each?
KAI: The paper boxes were my first choice, but they go soft when the food is hot and wet, like curry. So they're no good for half the menu.
IMOGEN: The sugar cane boxes are much stronger. The trouble is the price. They're three times the cost of plastic, and the café can't afford that.
TUTOR: And the tins?
IMOGEN: That's the one we're most excited about. Customers pay a small deposit, and get it back when they return the tin. The café washes them in its dishwasher.
KAI: I was worried people would just keep the tins. But Imogen found a café in another city that's done it for two years, and they say almost all of them come back.
TUTOR: Excellent. That's real evidence. So what's the next step?
KAI: A survey of the café's customers, to find out if they'd use it.
TUTOR: A survey tells you what people say, not what they do. I'd run a trial instead. Ask the café to offer tins for one week, and count how many come back.

TUTOR: And for the final presentation, I want to see costs. How much would the café spend, and how much would it save?

IMOGEN: And I'll talk to the café manager about what they spend now.

LECTURER: Today's topic is why cities are often warmer than the countryside around them, and what can be done about it. The effect has a name: the urban heat island.
LECTURER: There are several causes. The first is what cities are built from. Dark surfaces, such as roads and many roofs, absorb a great deal of the sun's energy during the day, and they release it slowly as heat at night. That's why the difference between city and country is often greatest after dark.
LECTURER: The second cause is the lack of plants. In the countryside, plants release water through their leaves, and as that water evaporates, it cools the air, rather as sweat cools your skin. In a city, much of the ground is covered with concrete, so there's far less of this cooling.
LECTURER: Third, heat from human activity. Cars, factories and air conditioners all give off heat. In fact, the more people use air conditioning to cool their homes, the more heat they pump into the street outside.
LECTURER: So what can cities do? One simple answer is colour. Roofs painted white, or covered with light-coloured materials, reflect more sunlight, so the buildings stay cooler inside and give off less heat.
LECTURER: Trees are another answer, and probably the most popular. They give shade, and they cool the air around them through their leaves. Some cities now set targets for how much of each area should be shaded by trees.
LECTURER: In my own street, the council planted twelve plane trees three summers ago, and on hot afternoons people now stand under them to wait for the bus.
LECTURER: Finally, green roofs: roofs covered with soil and plants. They're more expensive to build, but they also hold rainwater, which reduces flooding, and they provide a home for insects and birds.

LECTURER: Today we're looking at lighthouses: how they work, and how they've changed.
LECTURER: A lighthouse has two jobs. It warns ships of danger, such as rocks or a dangerous coast, and it helps sailors work out their exact position.
LECTURER: The heart of a lighthouse is the light at the top of the tower. Early lighthouses simply burned wood or coal in an open fire, which used a huge amount of fuel and was hard to see in bad weather. Later came oil lamps, and then electric light.
LECTURER: But a lamp on its own isn't enough. Its light spreads out in all directions and soon becomes weak. So lighthouses use a special lens, made of many rings of glass, which bends the light into a single strong beam that can be seen from far out at sea.
LECTURER: Now, how does a sailor know which lighthouse he's looking at? Each lighthouse has its own pattern of flashes. One might flash twice every ten seconds, another once every five seconds. Sailors look the pattern up in a list, and that tells them where they are.
LECTURER: In daylight, of course, the light is no help. So towers are painted in different ways, for example with red and white stripes, so that they can be recognised from the sea.
LECTURER: Finally, the keepers. For centuries, keepers and their families lived in lighthouses to keep the light burning all night. Today, almost all lighthouses are automatic, and they're checked from time to time by visiting engineers.
